sentences.text: Researchers used developing retinal bipolar cells to compare how cells move during different stages of tissue development.

Bipolar cells born before the photoreceptor layer forms move in a directed way that depends on microtubules, whereas later-born cells move in a more passive and less directed manner driven mainly by the movement of the surrounding tissue.
Blocking the movement of the whole tissue reduced the displacement of later-born cells, while preventing the formation of the photoreceptor layer caused these cells to move in a directed way.
Regardless of the movement strategy used, the bipolar cells ended up in the correct layer of the retina.
The findings suggest that the surrounding tissue environment can influence how cells move, a principle that may apply to other developing tissues.
